tests.note: The exact sentence matters: the checker compares characters, not meaning.

tests.note: Programme codes are printed as given, never expanded or title-cased.

tests.note: A middle name must survive: read the whole line, do not split and keep [0].

problems.starter:
name = input()
programme = input()
# print the slip

problems.title: Even attendance tally

tests.note: A single pass with an accumulator is enough; no sorting needed.
No even value is a valid answer: the count must be 0, not blank.
`-2 % 2` is 0 in Python, so negative even numbers belong in the tally.
Zero is even. A truthiness check (`if v`) silently drops it.

problems.starter:
n = int(input())
values = list(map(int, input().split()))
total = 0
count = 0
# add to total and count only for even values
print(total)
print(count)

problems.title: Second highest score

tests.note: A repeated top score is the same score, so the answer is 9 and not 9 from another index.
One distinct value means there is no second highest, so print NA.
`sorted()[1]` is wrong here only because repeats are not removed first.
A single score has no second place.
Starting your maximum at 0 breaks as soon as every score is negative.

problems.starter:
n = int(input())
scores = list(map(int, input().split()))
# second highest distinct value, or "NA"

problems.title: Word frequency in a notice

tests.note: Sorting by count alone leaves ties in insertion order; both keys are needed.

tests.input: a b b c c c
tests.note: A dictionary keeps counts fine; the order of printing is what you must control.
Lowercase before counting, otherwise LPU and lpu become two words.
One word still needs the `:count` suffix.

problems.starter:
words = input().split()
# lowercase, count, sort by (-count, word), then print word:count

problems.title: Transpose a seating grid

tests.note: The new row count is c, not r: swap the loops.
A square grid can hide a bug that only appears when r and c differ.
A 1x1 grid transposes to itself.

problems.starter:
r, c = map(int, input().split())
grid = [list(map(int, input().split())) for _ in range(r)]
# print r x c grid transposed

tests.note: Compare in one case only; M and m must match.

tests.input: A man, a plan, a canal: Panama
tests.note: Punctuation and spaces must be removed before comparing.
Digits are part of the text and do count.
Apostrophes are punctuation and must be dropped.
Nothing left to compare is a palindrome: that is a deliberate edge case.

problems.title: Balanced brackets

tests.note: Matching types, not just counts, is the rule.
Wrong order of closing: the top of the stack decides, not the next bracket.
A leftover stack at the end means unclosed brackets.
An empty line has nothing unclosed.
A closing bracket with an empty stack fails immediately.

problems.starter:
line = input()
# a list is a stack: append to push, pop to pop

problems.title: Fee pair reconciliation

tests.note: 2 + 4 is the pair; indices start at 0, so it prints 1 3.
Walk inward: when the sum is too small move the left pointer, too large move the right.
No pair means NA, not an empty line.
Equal values are allowed as a pair as long as the indices differ; a scan from both ends meets 0 and 3 first.
The smallest legal input still needs a printed answer.

problems.starter:
n = int(input())
amounts = list(map(int, input().split()))
target = int(input())
# two pointers from both ends

problems.title: Shift the invigilation roster

tests.note: Right rotation moves the last k to the front.
k = 0 is a legal no-op, and slicing must not produce an extra copy.
k greater than n must wrap: 6 mod 4 is 2.
5 mod 3 is 2, so the answer is Y Z X, not an index error.

problems.starter:
n, k = map(int, input().split())
roster = input().split()
# rotate right by k

problems.title: Next higher slot

tests.note: The 25 answers two positions at once: pop everything smaller when you meet it.
A strictly decreasing list has no next greater value at all.
The stack must keep indices, not values, or you cannot place the answers.
The last element never has a next greater value.

problems.starter:
n = int(input())
values = list(map(int, input().split()))
# monotonic stack, O(n)

problems.title: Queue from two stacks

tests.input:
6
push 1
push 2
front
pop
front
size
tests.note: FIFO: the first push must come out first, which a single stack cannot do.
Empty operations print EMPTY and must not raise.
After the queue drains, pop reports EMPTY again.

tests.input:
7
push 1
push 2
push 3
pop
push 4
pop
pop
tests.note: Items pushed after a pop must queue behind the ones already waiting.

problems.starter:
q = int(input())
# in_stack for pushes, out_stack for pops

problems.title: Merge two sorted sections

tests.note: Take the smaller head each step; do not sort again, and do not drop duplicates.
Equal values must both appear.
Interleaved duplicates catch a merge that advances only one side on equality.
An empty first list must still consume its (empty) line, or m is read from the wrong place.

problems.starter:
n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))[:n]
m = int(input())
b = list(map(int, input().split()))[:m]
# merge in one pass

problems.title: BST insert and traverse

tests.note: Inorder is sorted only because the tree is a BST; preorder starts at the root.
A single node has height 0, not 1.
Sorted input degenerates into a chain, which is the worst-case height.
Insertion order decides the shape, so a balanced-looking input is not sorted input.

problems.starter:
n = int(input())
keys = list(map(int, input().split()))
# build the tree, then traverse

problems.title: Group the anagrams

tests.input:
6
eat tea tan ate nat bat
tests.expected:
ate eat tea
bat
nat tan
tests.note: The key of a group is the word with its letters sorted.
Words inside a group are printed alphabetically, not in input order.
A repeated identical word belongs to the same group twice.
A single word is a group of one.
